items.description: Après plusieurs semaines de repos, les députés de l’Assemblée nationale de la République de Guinée ont repris leurs travaux à l’occasion de la session 2026-2027, au cours d’une grande cérémonie organisée dans la salle des Congrès du Palais du Peuple. À Conakry, la capitale guinéenne, de nombreuses délégations parlementaires venues de plusieurs pays d’Afrique de l’Ouest ont pris part à cet événement, marqué par des discours sur la coopération parlementaire et sécuritaire, ainsi que par des conférences-débats et des panels. Le président de l’Assemblée nationale de la République de Guinée, Dr Dansa Kourouma, a profité de son discours d’ouverture officielle de cette session pour exprimer, au nom des parlementaires, toute sa compassion aux nombreuses familles ayant perdu des proches lors de l’éboulement de Dar-Es-Salam. Survenu dans la nuit du 22 au 23 août dernier, ce drame a coûté la vie à 36 personnes, dont 17 de nationalité sierra-léonaise. Selon le président de l’institution, la représentation nationale n’a de sens que si elle partage les douleurs de ceux qu’elle représente. « Notre joie de ce jour ne saurait nous faire oublier les épreuves que notre peuple a traversées durant l’intersession : l’éboulement survenu à la décharge de Dar-es-Salam, à Conakry, des pluies diluviennes, les accidents mortels, etc. À la mémoire de toutes ces victimes, je vous invite à observer une minute de silence. Face à ces drames, la Nation a su se lever. L’État a pris ses responsabilités en matière de secours et de relogement. Nos partenaires, le secteur privé, les organisations communautaires et d’innombrables anonymes ont tendu la main. L’Assemblée nationale, ses élus en tête, a tenu à se tenir aux côtés des familles éprouvées, car la représentation nationale n’a de sens que si elle partage les douleurs de ceux qu’elle représente », a-t-il souligné. À toutes les familles endeuillées, le président a renouvelé la compassion et la solidarité de l’ensemble des députés. « Mais je veux aller plus loin. La compassion est un devoir; elle ne saurait être une politique. Lorsque les mêmes drames se répètent, la fatalité ne suffit plus à les expliquer. Il appartiendra à notre Assemblée, dans l’exercice de ses fonctions constitutionnelles de prendre la mesure et d’agir en toute responsabilité. Honorer nos morts, c’est aussi faire en sorte que de telles tragédies ne se reproduisent plus » Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Éboulement de Dar-Es-Salam : Dr Dansa Kourouma appelle à tirer les leçons du drame pour éviter de nouvelles tragédies est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: E-paiement : BAM abaisse à 0,5 % le plafond de la commission sur les cartes bancaires marocaines
items.description: Bank Al-Maghrib (BAM) a décidé de ramener, à partir du 1er octobre 2026, à 0,5 % le plafond de la commission perçue par les banques et les établissements de paiement lors des transactions effectuées par carte bancaire marocaine sur le territoire national. Cette mesure, qui fait suite à un premier encadrement de ces commissions fixé à 0,65 %, prévoit également un plafond spécifique de 0,15 % pour les commerces de proximité et les paiements gouvernementaux, a indiqué la Banque centrale dans une vidéo pédagogique diffusée sur sa chaîne officielle. Dans cette vidéo intitulée « Les avantages des moyens de paiement électroniques » , la Banque centrale rappelle qu'elle est l'institution chargée de veiller à la sécurité des systèmes de paiement au Maroc, y compris ceux liés à la carte bancaire. Pour illustrer le mécanisme, BAM prend l'exemple d'un achat réglé par carte chez un boulanger. Le montant est d'abord débité du compte du client, puis transféré à celui du commerçant, après déduction d'une commission au profit de l'établissement de paiement qui fournit le terminal de paiement électronique (TPE). Cette commission couvre notamment le coût des moyens techniques mis à la disposition du commerçant, le traitement des opérations et d'autres services. La banque du client, émettrice de la carte, perçoit pour sa part une commission de 0,15 % lorsque le commerce relève de la catégorie des commerces de proximité, et de 0,5 % dans les autres cas, précise la même source. Avant le 1er octobre 2024, le taux de cette commission n'était pas plafonné. Il a ensuite été encadré par Bank Al-Maghrib, avant d'être abaissé à partir du 1er octobre 2026, afin de permettre un accès sécurisé des commerçants et de la clientèle bancaire au paiement électronique. Selon la Banque centrale, cette évolution profite à l'ensemble des acteurs. Le commerçant voit ses charges diminuer, ce qui l'incite à accepter les paiements par carte quel que soit le montant, et peut ainsi stimuler ses ventes sans dépendre des liquidités disponibles en boutique. Le consommateur, lui, pourra trouver des TPE dans un plus grand nombre de points de vente, gagnant en temps et en confort dans ses transactions quotidiennes. The post E-paiement : BAM abaisse à 0,5 % le plafond de la commission sur les cartes bancaires marocaines appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Niger : Carburant – le déficit de super explose à 196,62 millions de litres en 2026, le gasoil sous surveillance…
items.description: Le Niger accuse, sur les huit premiers mois de 2026, un déficit de 196,62 millions de litres de supercarburant et de 52,60 millions de litres de gasoil, a annoncé, lundi 5 octobre, le ministre du Pétrole, M. Amadou Tini, devant la plénière du Conseil consultatif de la refondation (CCR). Selon le ministre, le super est devenu « le principal facteur de tension » du dispositif national d’approvisionnement. Le déficit est passé de 47,25 millions de litres en 2024 à 159,74 millions en 2025, avant d’atteindre 196,62 millions de litres rien que de janvier à août 2026, dépassant ainsi le niveau de toute l’année précédente. Pour le gasoil, la situation s’est également dégradée : après un solde négatif de 24,39 millions de litres en 2024, puis un léger excédent de 9,44 millions en 2025, un déficit de 52,60 millions de litres est apparu sur les huit premiers mois de 2026. Importations croissantes, pression financière sur la SONIDEP M. Tini a alerté sur le recours accru aux importations, qui deviennent « une composante de plus en plus importante de l’approvisionnement du marché ». Or, ces produits sont souvent acquis à un coût supérieur au prix de cession intérieur de la SORAZ, ce qui risque d’accroître la pression sur la trésorerie de la SONIDEP, déjà fragilisée par une dette record de 418 milliards de FCFA envers la raffinerie de Zinder. « Le problème n’est pas simplement de savoir si le Niger produit ou importe suffisamment de carburant. Il est de parvenir à un équilibre durable entre la production nationale, les importations, les stocks, la consommation réelle, les mouvements transfrontaliers, le niveau des prix et la capacité financière de la SONIDEP », a-t-il insisté. Le ministre a également dressé un tableau contrasté des autres produits pétroliers : GPL : les ressources recensées sont passées de 69 400 tonnes en 2023 à plus de 90 400 tonnes en 2025, avec une part d’importations oscillant entre 28,4% et 39,3%. Le coût moyen des importations a baissé, de 809 FCFA/kg en 2025 à environ 670 FCFA/kg en 2026, alors que le prix de revente reste fixé à 180 FCFA/kg. Jet A1 : entièrement importé, ses volumes ont chuté de 53 400 m³ en 2023 à environ 14 300 m³ au 30 septembre 2026, avant de se stabiliser. La filière algérienne est désormais privilégiée pour sécuriser cet approvisionnement. Pétrole lampant : les importations progressent régulièrement, de 627 m³ en 2023 à environ 985 m³ au 30 septembre 2026. La raffinerie de Zinder (SORAZ), avec une capacité installée de 20 000 barils/jour, livre environ 1,5 million de litres par jour à la SONIDEP. Son rendement moyen est de 86%, avec une répartition de 55% de gasoil, 26% d’essence et 5% de GPL. « Cette capacité installée n’est pas une capacité disponible tous les jours de l’année », a rappelé le ministre, soulignant que la SORAZ « reste indispensable » mais ne peut, à elle seule, couvrir la demande nationale. Un signal d’alerte, pas une accusation automatique M. Tini a tenu à préciser que les écarts entre les livraisons de la SORAZ et les sorties de la SONIDEP « ne doivent pas être interprétés automatiquement comme des volumes fraudés ou sortis clandestinement du territoire ». Ils constituent avant tout « un signal d’alerte » à croiser avec la production, les stocks, les importations, les ventes par zone, la consommation intérieure et les mouvements transfrontaliers. Parmi les facteurs explicatifs, il a cité la reprise de l’activité économique, l’évolution de la demande, le ravitaillement de véhicules étrangers, les mouvements vers les zones frontalières et d’éventuelles sorties irrégulières. « L’enjeu est donc de mesurer précisément la destination réelle des volumes », a-t-il conclu. Source: ANP L’article Niger : Carburant – le déficit de super explose à 196,62 millions de litres en 2026, le gasoil sous surveillance… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Ayawaso West Assembly cracks down on unauthorised market near Villagio
items.description: The Ayawaso West Municipal Assembly Task Force has taken action following the emergence of an unauthorised market at the Tetteh Quashie Roundabout near Villagio. The development comes months after the demolition of the Tetteh Quarshie Art Market and several adjoining businesses in the area by unidentified men in military-style uniforms. The March 2026 demolition sparked confusion and outrage among traders, with Deputy Minister for Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, Yussif Jajah, condemning the exercise and calling for an investigation. “Even if you have the power to take over this land, let the people take their valuables before you destroy the whole place,” he said at the time. Months after the demolition, affected artisans at the Ayawaso West Art Market said they were struggling with mounting debts, declining sales and difficulties supporting their families. The Assembly had relocated the traders to a temporary site near the original market, but some complained about poor patronage and difficulties caused by the rainy season. They also appealed for compensation and a permanent trading space. One trader said he lost more than GH¢30,000, while a master carver said he had incurred more than GH¢50,000 in debt after purchasing stock on credit. The Assembly’s NADMO Deputy Director for Technical, Eric Adjei Affum, said the Assembly was working to provide relief packages for affected traders, while acknowledging that the support would not fully compensate them for their losses. The emergence of another unauthorised market at the Tetteh Quashie Roundabout has renewed concerns about informal trading and the use of public spaces in the area. The enclave around the Tetteh Quashie interchange and Villaggio has in recent years experienced various forms of informal commercial activity, including street hawking and makeshift trading structures. The latest intervention by the Assembly is therefore part of its broader enforcement efforts against unauthorised developments and activities within the municipality. In October 2025, the Assembly arrested four people who allegedly claimed to be national security operatives and attempted to interfere with a demolition exercise near the Bawaleshie traffic light. The Assembly has also issued notices to owners of unapproved developments to regularise their building permits, warning of possible demolition and prosecution for non-compliance. The latest action at Tetteh Quashie, however, raises a familiar question for authorities: how to enforce planning regulations while addressing the livelihoods of traders who depend on informal spaces for their businesses.

items.title: Merz fait de l'Allemagne une cible pour la Russie, avertit la leader de l'AfD
items.description: Le 6 octobre, Alice Weidel, copresidente du parti d'extreme droite Alternative pour l'Allemagne (AfD), a critique le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz, dont les actions, selon elle, entraînent Berlin dans un conflit avec Moscou. Le dirigeant allemand « ne sait pas faire en sorte que l'Allemagne ne soit pas une cible pour la Russie », a-t-elle remarque, soulignant : « Cela doit cesser immediatement. Nous avons besoin de responsabilite ». D'apres Weidel, le conflit en Ukraine est devenu « un risque pour la securite, avant tout pour les Europeens et au premier chef pour la Republique federale d'Allemagne ». Elle a egalement qualifie avec sarcasme Merz de « chancelier des Affaires etrangeres » et de « meilleur chancelier que nous ayons jamais eu ». De plus, la dirigeante de l'AfD a condamne les promesses faites par le chancelier allemand a Volodymyr Zelensky d'octroyer de nouveaux milliards d'euros, alors que, selon elle, l'Allemagne manque d'argent « litteralement pour tout ». Elle a indique que Berlin avait deja investi 100 milliards d'euros en Ukraine, sans que la partie allemande n'ait recu le moindre rapport sur la maniere dont ces fonds avaient ete utilises. Friedrich Merz, arrive le 4 octobre a Kiev pour une visite inopinee, a immediatement essuye une vague de critiques. Maria Zakharova, porte-parole du ministere russe des Affaires etrangeres, a qualifie ce deplacement de « publicite faite sur le sang » , ajoutant : « Les meurtriers reviennent sur les lieux du crime. » Dans le meme temps, Alice Weidel a denonce le chancelier allemand, qui, en plein Jour de l'unite allemande, promettait a Kiev « de nouveaux milliards provenant des impots des contribuables allemands, qui font defaut pour financer les retraites et le systeme de sante, alors que l'Allemagne traverse la plus grave crise energetique de son histoire ». Ces critiques interviennent dans un contexte marque par une succession d'echecs politiques tant pour Friedrich Merz que pour son parti, l'Union chretienne-democrate d'Allemagne (CDU). L'une des raisons en est une serie de defaites aux elections regionales : son parti a ete battu par Alternative pour l'Allemagne au Mecklembourg-Pomeranie-Occidentale et en Saxe-Anhalt . La cote de popularite de Merz en a egalement pâti : au printemps, cet indicateur est tombe a 13 %, ce qui lui a valu le titre de dirigeant le moins populaire du pays. De plus, le 3 octobre, la popularite du bloc regroupant le parti de Friedrich Merz, l'Union chretienne-democrate d'Allemagne (CDU) et l'Union chretienne-sociale (CSU), a egalement chute a 18 %, atteignant son plus bas niveau historique. Dans ce contexte, selon les medias, plusieurs gouvernements de pays de l'UE auraient deja commence a se preparer a un eventuel depart de Friedrich Merz.

items.title: Enfant kidnappé à Yaoundé: la suspecte arrêtée à Tahoua
items.description: En fuite après l’enlèvement d’une mineure à Yaoundé, une femme, présentée comme la principale suspecte, a été interpellée le 5 octobre 2026 à Tahoua, au Niger, à l’issue d’une opération menée conjointement par les forces de sécurité camerounaises et nigériennes. La jeune fille a été retrouvée saine et sauve. La cavale aura finalement pris fin à Tahoua. Recherchée dans le cadre d’un enlèvement de mineure commis à Yaoundé, au Cameroun, une femme a été appréhendée, le lundi 5 octobre 2026, par les services de sécurité nigériens. La victime, qui avait été enlevée quelques jours plus tôt, a pu être libérée sans heurt. Dans un communiqué rendu public, le mardi 6 octobre 2026, la Police nationale du Niger a détaillé les circonstances de cette opération transfrontalière, menée en coordination avec les services de sécurité camerounais. Les faits remontent au 22 septembre 2026, dans la capitale camerounaise. Une jeune fille mineure avait alors été enlevée par des individus qui, peu après, avaient exigé une rançon de six millions de francs CFA. Les communications liées à cette demande avaient été effectuées à partir d’un numéro de téléphone localisé au Niger. Alertées, la Division Mœurs et Protection des Mineurs de la Direction de la Police Judiciaire (DPJ) au Cameroun et le Service de Police Judiciaire et Administrative (SPJA) de la région de Tahoua ont conjugué leurs efforts pour retrouver la victime et identifier les auteurs présumés. Le recoupement des informations recueillies au cours des investigations a permis aux enquêteurs de remonter progressivement la piste des ravisseurs. Les recherches ont notamment conduit à l’identification d’un relais présumé dans la ville de Tahoua. L’opération menée, le lundi 5 octobre, a finalement permis l’interpellation de la principale suspecte, présentée comme l’auteure présumée du rapt, ainsi que la libération de la mineure, saine et sauve. Pour la Police nationale du Niger, cette opération illustre l’importance de la coopération entre les services de sécurité dans la lutte contre les réseaux criminels opérant au-delà des frontières. Elle intervient également dans un contexte particulier, marqué par la rentrée scolaire et le retour des enfants sur les trajets entre leurs domiciles et leurs établissements. Les forces de sécurité appellent, par ailleurs, les parents, les enseignants et les encadreurs à renforcer la vigilance autour des enfants. Elles recommandent, notamment, de leur apprendre à ne jamais suivre un inconnu sans l'accord préalable d'un responsable, à respecter les règles élémentaires de sécurité sur les trajets domicile-école et à signaler tout comportement inhabituel. La Police invite enfin les familles à rester attentives aux confidences des enfants et à saisir rapidement les services compétents en cas de doute ou de disparition. Au-delà de cette interpellation, les autorités sécuritaires rappellent que la protection des mineurs repose aussi sur la vigilance collective. En cette période de rentrée scolaire, elles exhortent donc les familles et l’ensemble de la communauté éducative à redoubler de prudence afin de prévenir de nouvelles tentatives d’enlèvement. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Enfant kidnappé à Yaoundé: la suspecte arrêtée à Tahoua est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Burkina Faso: La production céréalière, en hausse de 53 %, couvre 124 % des besoins nationaux (ministre)
items.description: Selon des informations de l’Agence d’Information du Burkina (AIB), la production céréalière nationale du Burkina Faso a enregistré un bond spectaculaire de 53 %, passant de 4,66 millions de tonnes avant le lancement de l’Offensive agropastorale et halieutique à 7,14 millions de tonnes en 2025. Révélés par le ministre en charge de l’Agriculture, le commandant Ismaël Sombié, lors de la 3ᵉ édition des Journées nationales d’engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne (JEPPC), ces chiffres inédits permettent aujourd'hui au pays de couvrir 124 % de ses besoins céréaliers nationaux. Le Burkina Faso franchit un cap décisif sur la voie de la souveraineté alimentaire. D'après les données rapportées par l’Agence d’Information du Burkina (AIB), la production céréalière globale du pays est passée de 4,66 millions de tonnes avant le démarrage de l’Offensive agropastorale et halieutique à 7,14 millions de tonnes au cours de l'année 2025. Cette nette progression de 53 % permet désormais au Burkina Faso de couvrir 124 % de ses besoins céréaliers nationaux. Des récoltes historiques tirées par le riz et le maïs L'annonce a été faite par le ministre en charge de l'Agriculture, le commandant Ismaël Sombié, lors d’un panel organisé dans le cadre de la 3ᵉ édition des Journées nationales d’engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne (JEPPC), placée sous le thème : « Du champ au marché : produire et consommer burkinabè pour renforcer notre souveraineté ». Détaillant la structure de ces récoltes, le ministre a révélé que la production de riz paddy a dépassé pour la toute première fois la barre symbolique du million de tonnes, atteignant 1 008 737 tonnes en 2025. Dans le même temps, la production de maïs s'est établie à 2 686 531 tonnes. Maîtrise de l'eau, mécanisation et achats de souveraineté Ces résultats ont été soutenus par des investissements majeurs dans la maîtrise de l’eau, l'aménagement des terres, la mécanisation et la mise à disposition d'intrants. Au total, 11 774 hectares de périmètres irrigués ainsi que 41 275 hectares de bas-fonds ont été aménagés sur l'ensemble du territoire. Au-delà de la récolte, la stratégie gouvernementale a intégré le renforcement des maillons de collecte et de transformation. Plus de 350 000 tonnes de céréales ont ainsi été rachetées directement aux producteurs durant la campagne 2025-2026, portant les stocks de souveraineté nationale à plus de 380 000 tonnes. Plus de 839 milliards de FCFA mobilisés pour la phase 2 (2026-2028) Afin de consolider ces acquis, le gouvernement déploie la deuxième phase du programme, rebaptisée « Offensive agropastorale, hydraulique et halieutique 2026-2028 ». Évalué à 839,99 milliards de FCFA, ce plan prévoit l’aménagement supplémentaire de 50 000 hectares de périmètres irrigués et de 100 000 hectares de bas-fonds. Selon le commandant Ismaël Sombié, l'ambition centrale est de renforcer l'ensemble de la chaîne de valeur, de la production à la consommation, afin de réduire la dépendance extérieure, de créer des emplois et d'asseoir définitivement la souveraineté alimentaire du pays. L’article Burkina Faso: La production céréalière, en hausse de 53 %, couvre 124 % des besoins nationaux (ministre) est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Lastec CEO Lasisi Oseni nominated for Ghana Auto Fix Award
items.description: Chief Executive Officer of Lastec Auto Centre in Amasaman, Accra, Lasisi Oseni, has been nominated for the Collision Repairs Expert Award at the upcoming Ghana Auto Fix Awards. The nomination recognises his work in vehicle collision repairs and restoration at the auto centre, which provides services including accident repairs, diagnostics, bodywork and servicing. Mr. Oseni says the nomination is a recognition of the hard work that has gone into building his business. “It is a recognition of the hard work we have put into the business over the years, and I am truly humbled by the nomination,” he said. He says the automotive repair industry is changing, with modern vehicles requiring specialised diagnostic equipment, software knowledge and continuous technical training. Mr. Oseni has invested in upgrading his workshop, including the purchase of a spraying oven to improve the quality of vehicle bodywork and painting. He says the nomination will encourage him and his team to continue improving their services. Mr. Oseni started his career in the automotive repair business after developing an interest in vehicle mechanics and gradually building experience in the trade. He later established Lastec Auto Centre, which has grown into a workshop offering a range of vehicle repair and maintenance services. His journey has also involved significant personal investment in the business. At one point, he sold his Mercedes-Benz E-Class to raise funds to purchase equipment for the workshop. Members of the public can vote for Lasisi Oseni by dialling * 447 *165#, following the prompts and entering nominee code 32.

items.title: Polo Beach Club land belongs to La Traditional Council, not Labadi Beach Hotel – Freddie Blay
items.description: Former National Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Freddie Blay, has disputed the ownership basis for the demolition of the Polo Beach Club, insisting that the land belongs to the La Traditional Council rather than the Labadi Beach Hotel. Speaking in an exclusive interview with JoyNews following the demolition of the facility last week, Mr Blay said his son secured an agreement from the traditional authority before developing the facility. According to him, his son initially approached the Labadi Beach Hotel about acquiring the land but was directed by the hotel to the La Traditional Council. “My son had the rights, his company discussed it with the La Traditional Council, before he went there (to the traditional authority), he approached them (the Labadi Beach Hotel) and talked about taking a piece of that place to develop it alongside them because it involved certain logistics, bathrooms, toilets, packing space and therefore let us do it together and share the profit, “ “They, the Labadi Beach authority, told him (his son) it (the land) doesn’t belong to us; it belongs to the La Beach Management Organisation,” he claimed the hotel told his son. Mr Blay said his son subsequently reached an agreement with the traditional authority to develop the site. He argued that the development followed engagements with the relevant parties rather than an arbitrary occupation of the land. “In one instance, I accompanied him (his son) to the La Traditional Council, and they agreed, negotiated and gave him a lease over that place to set it (Polo Beach Club) up,” he argued. He expressed surprise that the facility had now been demolished on the basis that the land belonged to the Labadi Beach Hotel. “Now what happens is that, out of ignorance, some people are saying that the place belongs to La Beach Hotel and that other people, including my son, are squatters; they are not squatters. Take it from me that La Beach Hotel has taken my son’s company to court; issues were set up for the trial as to whether they are just encroachers,” “They (the Hotel) realised that the case was going against them, so they quickly withdrew,” he added. The Polo Beach Club was demolished on Friday, October 2, 2026, during a clearance operation along the La beachfront involving personnel from the Ghana Armed Forces’ 48 Engineer Regiment and the Ghana Police Service. READ ALSO : Freddie Blay accuses government of politically motivated demolitions targeting his family Deputy Chief of Staff in charge of Operations, Stan Dogbe, said the operation was conducted under National Security supervision following a request from the Labadi Beach Hotel. According to Mr Dogbe, the hotel had raised concerns that structures and commercial activities along the beachfront were affecting its safety, tranquillity and reputation, as well as the experience of its visitors. He clarified that the operation was separate from the government’s flood mitigation programme. Mr Blay had previously questioned why the demolition proceeded while the land dispute remained before the courts. In comments reported on October 3, he maintained that his son had acquired the land from the La Stool and challenged suggestions that the business was occupying the site unlawfully.

items.title: ‘Don’t speculate’ – Upper West Minister charges SOCO facilitators as project delivers 127 projects, 173 more underway
items.description: The Upper West Regional Minister, Charles Lwanga Puozuing, has issued a strong warning to newly recruited Community Facilitators under the Gulf of Guinea Northern Regions Social Cohesion (SOCO) project, urging them to stop speculating and seek clarification from Municipal and District Assemblies when they need information. Speaking at an engagement in Wa, the Minister charged the facilitators to own the opportunity and become true ambassadors of accurate information in their communities. “When you are concerned about an issue, do not speculate or provide information based on assumptions. Seek clarification from the appropriate District Assembly officials,” he stressed. Mr Puozuing described the facilitator role as more than just a job, saying it was an opportunity for personal development and community transformation. He urged the facilitators to save and invest part of their earnings. “Save part of your earnings, invest in a productive activity, develop a useful skill. We want the benefits to extend beyond this assignment,” he added. The Minister reminded the facilitators that the government and the World Bank were investing $150 million in 48 assemblies across six northern regions to prevent conflict spillover from the Sahel and improve livelihoods. Meanwhile, the SOCO Zonal Coordinator for Upper West and Savannah, David Yankey, revealed significant progress under the project. Under Cycle 1, the project delivered 127 sub-projects, including schools, CHPS compounds, roads and libraries, across all 11 districts in the Upper West Region and selected districts in the Savannah Region. Cycle 2 is even larger, with 173 sub-projects, including JHS blocks, primary schools, nursery blocks and clinics, currently under construction. Mr Yankey explained that the facilitators would serve as a critical link between communities, District Assemblies and the Ministry. They would help ensure that community needs captured in Action Plans were reflected in the projects delivered by the government, while also supporting the recruitment of local youth for construction jobs. The project is also going fully digital. According to the Management Information Systems Specialist, Richard Adofo Ansong, SOCO has deployed the SOCO App for data collection in the field, alongside a SOCO Management Information System (MIS) that serves as a repository for high-level decision-making. To handle complaints, all World Bank projects are required to have a grievance redress mechanism. SOCO is using the Single Window Citizen Engagement Service (SWCES) operated by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection for this purpose.

items.title: DG ISPR says Pakistani troops present in Saudi Arabia 'for decades' across multiple domains
items.description: Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that Pakistani troops are in Saudi Arabia, adding that they had been in the kingdom “for decades” and across multiple domains. The military spokesperson made these remarks during an interview with CNN correspondent Ivan Watson, who posted a small clip on his X account. “I can confirm that the forces of Pakistan are already there (Saudi Arabia),” Lt Gen Chaudhry said. Watson then sought a confirmation that Pakistani troops were already on the ground in Saudi Arabia as part of the Makkah Defence Alliance between Pakistan, the kingdom and Turkiye. To that, the military spokesperson replied, “Pakistan troops have been there for decades […] The Makkah alliance is not something that has come out in a vacuum. So there is a sustained diplomatic, political, military and people-to-people relationship between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia. So, I can share with you that Pakistani forces, in multiple capabilities and domains, are already there.” Lt Gen Chaudhry’s remarks come after Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye agreed to the deployment of military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Riyadh on Monday. The three countries had held an emergency meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) of the Makkah Defence Alliance to address the security developments and threats facing Saudi Arabia. “The committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats,” a statement issued by the Foreign Office after the meeting said. While the statement did not specifically name any threat, the development comes against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in the Yemen conflict. Separately, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and said Saudi Arabia had made “gains and recovered some areas” in Yemen in the ongoing fighting with the Houthis. When asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, the defence minister replied that both nations had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. “Whatever assistance they require is being provided. But right now, the Turkish and Pakistani armies are playing a supportive role,” he said, noting that Pakistan was involved in reconnaissance. Asif had earlier also reaffirmed that Pakistan would “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalated. The defence minister had said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. The Makkah defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. On Sept 25, the military chiefs of alliance members Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh for urgently convened talks under the pact in light of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sept 18, Lt Gen Chaudhry had expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying Pakistan will go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”.

items.title: Why American Cities Cost So Much and Deliver So Little
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on the sudden recall of 12 B-1 bombers from their base in the south of England to the mainland of the United States. He asks what prompted the move and why the Trump administration refuses to learn vital military lessons from Ukraine. Then, David is joined by Reihan Salam, the president of the Manhattan Institute for Policy Research, to discuss why American cities cost so much and often deliver so little. They explore how some urban governments waste public money, how cities could provide better services to residents, and why the rise of populism is doing little to solve Americans’ actual problems. Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of Every War Must End by Fred Charles Iklé. The following is a transcript of the episode: Reihan Salam: Well, David, I actually don’t believe that it is Donald Trump who is the only political figure who will have been discredited by this moment. When you’re looking at the Democratic coalition right now, I see a lot of anger and frustration with how people see their leadership class as well. So I think that this is going to be this big generational turnover that could go very badly. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Reihan Salam, president of the Manhattan Institute, and we’ll discuss how American cities can deliver better government to their residents at more reasonable costs than they now do. This week’s book will be a masterpiece of strategic thinking: Every War Must End by Fred Charles Iklé. But before either the dialogue or the book discussion, some opening thoughts on a news story you may have seen this past weekend: the sudden recall of 12 B-1 bombers from their base in the south of England to the mainland of the United States. As so often with Trump-administration military stories, there may be less, or there may be more, to this story than meets the eye. The Trump administration is staffed by people who look for any opportunity and any excuse to recall military assets from allies, and especially from European allies, back to the American mainland. This recall may be something that people in the Trump administration wanted to do anyway, for their own reason. And we’ll find out more about that in the days ahead. But the first reports may also be true—that there was some sudden threat to these bombers that necessitated their removal from England back to the American mainland. What might that threat be? Either a terrorist attack in Britain, or else possibly a drone-and-missile attack like those that have been experienced by American forces in the Persian Gulf. We don’t know. But what we do know is that through the Persian Gulf, the Iranians have had great success, much greater success than as first reported, pushing back American forces from their perimeters. The American naval base in Bahrain was badly damaged by Iranian drones and missiles. As we have seen in Ukraine, suddenly individuals far from the battle scene controlling these small, comparatively inexpensive new technologies can inflict tremendous damage anywhere on the enemy’s territory. The Ukrainians have done it to Russia, and the Russians have done it to the Ukrainians. We may be living through a revolution in military technology as dramatic as when the advent of gunpowder made obsolete the knight on horseback and the castle made of stone. The United States is poorly adapted to this revolution, and especially poorly adapted under the Trump administration. There are deep reasons why the United States is poorly adapted to this revolution. The United States has made an enormous investment in very costly, very sophisticated platforms: bombers, fighters, aircraft carriers, tanks, equipment. Machinery that moves aboveground, on the land, on the ocean, in the air. And it is reluctant to accept that this enormous investment may now be obsolete, and obsolete in ways that empower weaker adversaries who master the new technology of drone warfare first. The United States is also poorly adapted because of the way America finances and approves its military technology. The congressional system—the iron triangle of lobbyists and administrations and Congress—tends to regard weapons as not just tools of war, but also as tools of economic development back at home, and oftentimes as income-support strategies for retired members of the military. And so the United States invests very deeply in systems that are driven by domestic needs and not by the needs of the battlefield. In the Trump era, these difficulties are augmented by two special problems. The first is the nation that is the pioneer and leader in drone warfare is Ukraine. And the United States under President Trump is terribly reluctant, brutally reluctant, to learn lessons of war from Ukraine. President Trump, Vice President Vance, and others around them decided early that the Ukrainians were losers, that they were doomed, that they were dependents, they were welfare recipients, they were moochers, they deserved nothing, and they had nothing to offer. Now it turns out they may be the leading military innovator of the modern era, and suddenly it’s very embarrassing to turn around and say, maybe these guys, of whom the Trump administration has so little good to say, maybe they have something to offer that America needs. So the reluctance to learn lessons from Ukraine—and the eagerness to fire the generals and admirals most ready to learn the lessons from Ukraine—that has handicapped the United States. There’s another handicap in the drone-warfare era, and that is ideological. Secretary Hegseth is a man with a vision of the military as a tool for waging culture war, not real battlefield warfare. He has inveighed against troops who wear beards, against troops who are overweight, against troops who don’t have enough testosterone. He wants to promote troops that look a certain way, that can do certain physical exercises. It is said in a new Rolling Stone profile of just-retired Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll that Hegseth’s vision is of an army that is ready for Instagram, not ready for war. And as he systematically goes through the army, firing those generals who want to learn the lessons of the new, Hegseth has left the United States vulnerable to the lessons of the new. My wife’s grandfather was the founder of the Canadian [Royal Army] Armoured Corps. He’s contested through his life with the old and outdated proponents of cavalry warfare. And he lamented: There’s something about senior military command that has the effect of transforming brain into bone. Something like that seems to be going on in the higher reaches of the Trump Defense Department. And it’s happened at a time when we desperately need all the brains we can get. As I said, there may be less or more to this story of B-1 bombers being recalled than first reported, but it is a portent of something ominous in the changing world of national security. Something ominous that this administration and this Department of War, so called, is uniquely unready to meet. And now my dialogue with Reihan Salam. [ Music ] Frum: Reihan Salam grew up in Brooklyn, the son of immigrants, and went through New York City’s public schools. He started out doing research for David Brooks at The New York Times, worked as a producer at NBC News, and became an editor at The Atlantic and National Review. In 2008, he and Ross Douthat co-authored Grand New Party : an argument that the GOP, the Republican Party, should do more to appeal to working-class voters. In 2018, he published Melting Pot or Civil War?, arguing for an immigration system built on skills. In 2019, he became the fifth president of the Manhattan Institute, carrying a warning to all conservatives that a conservatism that does not speak to cities will be marginalized. Canadian listeners: Be aware that Reihan also possesses an expert knowledge of Canadian politics. Reihan is an old and dear friend, and it’s a pleasure to welcome him to The David Frum Show. Reihan, welcome. Reihan Salam: Thank you for having me, David. It’s a pleasure to be with you. Frum: Well, let’s focus on your day job of city government. Back in the Reagan ’80s, there was a bumper sticker, a good-natured conservative joke: Thank God we don’t get all the government we pay for. I don’t know that New Yorkers or San Franciscans or Angelinos—they pay for a lot of government, a lot. And I think most of the inhabitants of these overwhelmingly Democrat blue cities would like to see more reward for the money they pay. This has been the work of the Manhattan Institute. It looks like in 2026 the country is going to veer to the left; maybe quite far to the left. State government, local government in these places is already pretty far to the left. Without telling anyone on the left not to be on the left—they wouldn’t listen—but how do people in New York, in Los Angeles, in San Francisco, in similar cities, get more of the government they’re already paying for? Salam: Well, fundamentally, when I think about a dense, large city, I do believe that it is reasonable to expect that you’re going to have a larger government. Density creates enormous opportunities; it creates enormous productivity. But it also creates demons of density as well, when you’re thinking about the need for more stringent policing, when you’re thinking about the other questions of urban management, public health. When you’re thinking about drainage, when you’re thinking about environmental pollutants. Any number of questions. So my starting point is that it is reasonable to expect that you’re going to have a more energetic government in these places. You need a more energetic government to fully unlock that potential of urban life. The problem, as you suggest, is that also that wealth that you create in these dynamic, productive cities also becomes a target for extraction. And though you might have the starting point as, Hey, we need to have a capable government to solve problems X, Y, and Z , another thing that can often happen, depending on the political dynamic in the city and whether or not you have meaningful competition and what have you—and we can get more into that—but basically, you have this dynamic where in many cases that wealth is being extracted by interest groups that become really potent and entrenched. So think about it this way. New York City employs 300,000 city employees. That is in some ways an undercount, because you have a lot of other people who are employed indirectly, who are subsidized by city and state government in various other ways. That is already a very potent political constituency unto itself. People who have a vested interest not only in a city government that is large, but also a city government that is offering very favorable terms of employment to its various employees. What do I mean by favorable term of employment? Well, let’s say you don’t necessarily want a very high degree of accountability. Let’s say you want very strong tenure rules. Let’s say you want the job to be a more attractive or appealing job according to various metrics, so that the job actually becomes more attractive than the equivalent job in the private sector. So you may well get featherbedding over time. You may well employ more people than you need to, strictly speaking. Or, you know, though, technically, we have civil service hiring and notionally we’re hiring people on a meritocratic basis, but it could be that that’s not quite how it happens. That you’re growing the city-employment rolls because you’re, again, trying to achieve some larger political objective. In New York City—and I think this applies to many other cities as well—you could think of this as the friction not between Republicans and Democrats, but call it Tammany Hall and reform. Tammany Hall being the politics of patronage, the politics of using public dollars, not necessarily solely to achieve a public purpose, but using public dollars to entrench and grow a given political coalition. And then, the party of reform—that again could come with a Democratic label or a Republican label or whichever label—that comes in to say, Okay, we’re going to take away the punch bowl. You know, We are going to be the ones who are going to refocus city government on what matters, on delivering efficiency . And I think that that is this oscillation of power that has been part of the American urban story. But it’s not unique to dynamics within the city. It also is shaped by dynamics outside of it, and larger cultural and political forces. Frum: I was in New York this past weekend. At one point in the weekend I was crawling along westward, inch by inch, on a Midtown street and observing: The reason the street was moving so slowly is because it was a three-lane street. One lane was being used for driving, and two lanes were being used for cheap parking. Who made that decision that the city should give two-thirds of the street away as a subsidized parking lot to the people using the street? So that’s a giveaway to somebody, or more or less randomly chosen people, but it’s still a giveaway. And I think everyone who drives along the street must have had the same question that I’ve done. And yet obviously it’s impossible to do anything about it, because there it is: Two-thirds of the street is used for subsidized parking. Salam: Well, we also know from the great scholar of parking, Donald Shoup, that actually quite a bit of that traffic consists of people who are looking for a parking spot. So, in a way, there’s many levels to this perversity. But, part of it is a point, it’s an observation that kind of answers itself. So when you become used to the entitlement, the expectation that you’re going to have free parking, moving from one equilibrium—which is a very painful and damaging one, that causes all kinds of waste, all kinds of economic damage—to a new one that may well be much more efficient, but you’re not necessarily going to be thinking, Think about all this time that I’ve saved. I feel so blessed, I feel so fortunate. What you’re going to think about is that: I once had an entitlement to free parking on the street, and now I don’t. Including if you’re not someone who drives especially often. You just could think in the back of your head, Aha, I once had this entitlement. And in New York City, and in many other cities besides, you also have these bespoke arrangements. You have what you might think of as these hereditary rights that you gain over time. So if you’re looking at many public employees in New York City, in many cases, they will use placards to identify themselves as public employees. And one reason they do that is to ensure that they will not receive tickets. Because the idea is that if you work in parking enforcement, if you are someone who is looking to a fellow public employee, you will treat them differently than you treat other people. Now, that hereditary privilege alone is something that actually has enormous effects on the flow of traffic. But it’s just one of many ways in which, when you’re thinking about any city, you’re not just thinking about a place that is run through cool rationality. You know, how are we thinking about the technocratic management of this urban landscape? You are thinking about traditions; you are thinking about this deference; you are thinking about this exercise of power in a lot of other ways that don’t actually rise to the level of being covered by the newspaper or even being understood in some data-rich kind of way. These are just the ways that things work that degrade the quality of life, but that people tolerate until they don’t. Frum: As blue cities and blue jurisdictions swing further to the left after November of 2026, which is what looks likely to happen, they are insisting that the solution is to capture more revenue, and especially to capture it from the very richest people. And so their projects—you see them in Washington state and other places—to impose an extra-heavy level of surtaxes on the very richest people in the jurisdiction, thinking that that’s the way out. That seems an ideological commitment. And it seems like a strange commitment for subnational governments to have, because it’s a country in which it’s very easy to move. It’s a world in which people have less and less reason that they have to be in any particular place. But it seems to be a move that urban governments are determined to make in 2026. Salam: I am a great believer in the potential of our great cities, and so I do believe that they are very attractive. They have many advantages, particularly when you’re thinking about an aging society. It is not difficult to imagine a world in which younger people in an aging society want to cluster with other younger people. So those are advantages, and I think a lot of people are taking those advantages and saying, Gosh, we can tax much more, we can allow the quality of services to degrade further. And that’s going to be fine; there will still be the stickiness of economic activity. I believe that’s a mistake, even though I do believe in that power of urban concentration, urban agglomeration, urban productivity. Because, as you suggest, I think that there are other forces on the other end. There are other cities that are emerging that are themselves competitive. But the larger point I would make is this, David. We have been living through a period of fiscal expansion and fiscal incontinence. You know that our deficits are above 6 percent of GDP right now. This is at a time when unemployment is 4.2 percent, quite low by historical standards. And yet, even then, we have this enormous deficit. And that deficit trickles into state and local governments. It trickles in, because you have your city budget funded by city taxes, but then you have your portion of the city budget funded by transfers from state governments. And then you have the proportion of the city and state governments funded by federal dollars as well. And this is really, really important to understand. Now you know as well as anyone, David, that a huge driver of employment in any American city, big or small, is what we affectionately refer to as “eds and meds.” The education system and the health system. These are two systems that are very heavily subsidized. The health system in particular is very heavily subsidized by federal dollars and, might I add, borrowed federal dollars. New York City might be a somewhat extreme case, but it’s not unique. But in New York City, 52 percent of residents are on either Medicaid or something called the Essential Plan, which is a Medicaid-like publicly subsidized health system. Now we can debate whether or not that’s strictly necessary. I would argue that it’s not. That in fact, if we had a narrower safety net, we would have more effective safety-net programs, and you’d have a lot of other folks who would find private health insurance, let’s say, and then you would have a somewhat lower burden, tax burden, and yada yada. Let’s come back to that for a moment. But fundamentally, you’re looking at a city that is a very dynamic city with a very dynamic private economy. But if you’re actually looking at employment, if you’re actually looking at the biggest, fastest-growing private-sector job in New York City, but also in many other cities besides, it is home health aids. Now that is a private-sector job in a sense, that you are not literally a public employment, but it is also a publicly subsidized job. And it’s a job in which you, David Frum, or I, Reihan Salam, if I were on a subsidized program and I have a subsidized home health aid, I’m not paying with my own dollars. And so in some cases, you might not actually have someone who is offering a service with value commensurate to what the public sector is paying for that service. That is something you are seeing more and more in American political economy, and particularly in our cities. Frum: Okay. Now I invite you to imagine a meeting that you are taking with one of the more leftish crop of new urban officials, local officials, in the country after of November of ’26. And the meeting begins with the person you’re talking to saying: Reihan Salam, you are a self-identified conservative. Conservatives are very out of style. A lot of the problems that that our city faces are driven by the Trump administration: its many forms of interference in our lives that were unasked for. Why should anybody listen to you? What can you possibly have to say that’s of value to me as I cope with my problems and my constituents? Salam: Well, I believe that fundamentally, whatever the partisan label, there are some underlying structural forces that are going to come to bite relatively soon. If you look at the urban-policy revolution that unfolded in the late ’80s, 1990s, 2000s, the big insight was not some grand ideological insight. It was this—it was that when you’re looking at a lot of major cities that had for many decades been begging the federal government for money— Give us more money to solve this problem . My old colleague Fred Siegel called this the riot ideology. If you do not give us money, there are going to be riots. You know, we’re not going to be able to control it; it’s going to be really bad. And therefore, you just kept going and rattled the tin cup, begging for more money from the federal government. The problem is when you have a federal government that starts to tighten its belt by necessity, then suddenly you’re going to have a more discerning federal government that’s going to be thinking about: Where exactly am I going to be applying these subsidy dollars? And it’s not necessarily going to be in a place that is not really politically contested. During the migrant crisis that unfolded during the Biden presidency, Mayor Eric Adams, a Democrat, was begging the Democratic president, Joe Biden, to rescue New York City by infusing more federal dollars into the city. And the Biden administration said no. The Biden administration said, You have a right to shelter. You have a ton of other policies that actually have exacerbated this crisis in your city. And by the way, we’re not really concerned about losing the five boroughs of New York City as voters in our upcoming presidential election, so we’re not going to be all that concerned about you. And that’s in a case where they were quite happy, as President Trump is, to run an enormous federal deficit. So basically what happened is you had an alternative to tin-cup politics. You had a group of mayors who said, We have to solve some of these problems ourselves. So you don’t have to listen to me. All you have to do is look at your bottom line. All you have to do is look at the fact that you’re going to start experiencing, if you haven’t already, very stringent budget constraints, and voters to whom you’ve been making a lot of promises that are going to be very hard to fulfill given this new fiscal landscape. Frum: Can we talk about schools for a moment? I mean, you in your own life owe so much to the schools as ways to identify and promote talent. And so much of your rise to your eminence was achieved because of the talent scouting that occurred in the New York public-school system. New York and other cities seem to be less interested in doing that. In fact, they seem to want to break a lot of the mechanisms for finding talent and helping talent forward. Why does that happen? Is there anything that can be done to change the cities? Or maybe the cities aren’t even wrong. Maybe the talent-scouting mechanism is too exclusionary and unfair. Salam: There’s so many things going on that are making our cities today really different than they were 30 years ago. So, narrowly on the education point, you know this as well as I do, David, in many big, urban public-school systems, it increasingly feels as though the system is being run for the benefit of the system’s employees than for its notional beneficiary students. That’s not because anyone is sinister. It’s because you’re seeing declining enrollment. That’s kind of one thing that is going on across jurisdictions. But also, you have the system that employs an enormous number of people who are themselves people who might feel economically fragile. These are people where some of them absolutely could find more remunerative employment outside of these public systems, but some of them are people who might not be able to find more remunerative employment outside of these systems. What we’ve been doing in the United States as a whole since the 1970s is, we’ve been increasing the amount of staff in our school systems. That is: We’re hiring more teachers, but we’re hiring more paraprofessionals as well. So if you’re looking at the staffing ratios, how many students do you have relative to the number of adult employees of the school system? You’ve seen a really dramatic change over this time. And so if you’re looking to people who are employed in public education, they will often say that, well: Look, education is part of our mission. But we also are providing meals. We are providing counseling. We have students in some cases who are homeless, who are suffering from various other maladies. And so we are essentially social-service bureaucracies in miniature that are serving this troubled population. Now, you know, we can get into that specifically, whether or not that’s a sound argument. But also think about a middle-class parent who, as you were suggesting before, has options. They don’t necessarily have to enroll their children in that school system. They can move elsewhere and what have you. That system that is leading with the idea that, well, Look, education schmeducation. Yes, this or that might be true—but how dare you not appreciate this incredibly profound social mission that we have? And by the way, gosh, you’re right, maybe we’re not doing as well as we might on the educational front, but that’s because of segregation and inequality and various other problems of cosmic injustice that we, of course, in our small little school system, can’t possibly solve on our own. So it becomes this incredible buck-passing to help cement the political coalition that allows for these failures to unfold. And again, there are some great people in these systems. There are some excellent schools within these systems. But the underlying logic is one that leads you to more excuse-making and away from accountability. Frum: Tell me what is wrong with the argument I’m about to present. A historic idea in the New York system—long ago, a generation ago and more—was, students in the school system are going to be disproportionately poor. Some of them are going to be very talented people who might not have on their own, from their own family resources, the opportunities that their talent could use, could benefit from, and could benefit all of us. So we’re going to do talent-sifting. We’re going to look for those talented 30 percent, and we’re going to promote them and fast-track them and help them to get to college and to discover things in themselves that the people in their lives, who they grow up with, may not recognize for them. That’s been a view in the past. It’s increasingly challenged. And we’ve all been reading with fascination the recent eruption between a famous New York Times writer and her daughter. The New York Times writer said to the daughter, You’re going to go to the same school as everybody else. And the daughter said, You have the ability to get me into a better school. Why won’t you help me? And the mother said, It’s a point of principle. What is wrong with what the mother is saying? And what is potentially right about the old way of doing it, or vice versa? Salam: Well, I believe the mother in that case was right to say that: My daughter has been failed by these schools, and there is something broken . Where she goes wrong is with her view as to what the right structural solution would be. So this is my answer to any number of dilemmas facing American cities, and it’s this: When you are an American city that has people who want to solve problems for you at very low fiscal cost to you, you should let them do it. What do we mean by that? So, one thing we hear again and again—you hear this in Los Angeles, New York City, Boston, San Francisco, of course, any number of cities—we have an acute housing crisis. And that’s true. We have an acute housing crisis in many American communities. But what you also have is a crisis that could present its own solution. In New York City, asking rents are so high for the tiny number of units that are available that there are people crazy enough that they will come along and say, I will build private rental housing, if you let me do it and if you allow me to charge what the market will bear. You might think they’re mad. I might think they’re mad, because there’s so many other barriers that you have to overcome, so many political obstacles. But if you let them do it, they would do that. In a similar vein, there are people who run school systems in New York City, in the five boroughs of New York City, but also in many other urban jurisdictions besides, who will say: Hey, I’m running a charter network. Give me a fraction. And by the way, they’d rather have more money, but they’ll say, Hey, give me 80 percent of what you’re giving to your public district schools for my public charter school, where I don’t have the same collective-bargaining rules and I have greater flexibility. And I can educate those students much more effectively. There are people who will solve that problem for you if you just let them solve it for you. So, to my friends on the left, what I would say is that, you have bigger fish to fry. You know, maybe you want to address the Middle East. You know, you want to address kind of various other problems. Why don’t you allow these other people to educate young people? And do it competitively and at reasonable cost. Why don’t you let these other people address this acute housing crisis, and you can focus, you know, much like the Queen of England, and now the King of England, is able to serve as defender of the faith and do other things, the magic and mysticism of kind of any any form of government. Why don’t you focus on those things and then allow these other people to solve the problem? Frum: I’m smiling at your joke. The new mayor of New York should focus on solving the problems of the Middle East and let volunteers deliver schools and build housing for him. Salam: Because they will do it. They will come along and do it if you actually just create a system. Frum: And because, well, he’s got a lot to say about the Middle East, of course, and everyone there wants to hear from him. Salam: And that seems to be, you know, kind of a burning passion for him and for many other people. And again, I might disagree with where he lands in the Middle East, but we’ll leave that aside. Frum: But he’s probably pretty harmlessly occupied talking about it. Salam: He might actually do less damage if he simply said, I’m going to actually serve as an ambassador for—I’m going to serve as a mascot for this or that political cause. But why don’t you create the systems that allow other actors, including in some cases public actors, to do good work. Frum: Well, you mentioned housing, and that was where I wanted to go next. You and I come from a tradition where we believe if you let private builders build tens of thousands of new units per year, even if all of those units are aimed at the top of the market, simply the presence of those tens of thousands a year of new units all aimed at the top of the market is going to push down prices all the way through the market. But that seems to be, at least in the city of New York, a discarded, rejected idea. And they say that if you build lots of units at the top of market, they will only serve the top of the market, and everything else will remain unchanged by the arrival of all of these new units. Can you speak up on behalf of what we used to think of as the basic economics of housing, against the new idea that no matter how many units you build at the top, it won’t change anything else for anybody else? Salam: It’s very simple. If you—right now, the way that we are approaching housing in many of our cities is, you’re saying that the desire to build private rental housing is suspect. It is something that is very questionable. We will allow you to do it if you do 15 other things to prove to us that you’re not actually doing something sinister or dubious or questionable or whatever else. So one thing we’ll say is that we’ll allow you to build private rental housing if you set aside some number of those new units to represent permanently affordable housing stock. That is to say—if you set it aside so that people with incomes below a certain threshold can afford these units, and then if you’ll do that on a kind of ongoing basis, then we’ll allow you to build some other private housing. But the funny thing there is that what you’re effectively doing is that these people who want to build more housing supply, you’re taxing them. You’re saying that: We’re actually going to limit the number of new market-rate units you can build, so that you can set aside this number of units that are mandatory below-market, affordable. So actually, you make it even harder to solve the bigger problem, which is that demand is outstripping supply. Then you could say, Well, we’ll allow you to build it, but you need to offer very high wages to the people building it. Because actually somehow this work, relative to all forms of work otherwise, needs to be put in some separate bucket. And we don’t trust those workers to be able to come to some arrangement with you, because you exert power—any number of, there are all of these other side deals that are imposed so that you actually see to it that the amount of new housing is a trickle. Now, actually, how it really works, when it works, is this: You allow a bunch of speculators to build, and indeed to overbuild, so that actually they eventually come to a point where they lose their shirts. And they, as investors, lose their shirts. It’s not the city government that loses its shirt through a subsidy; it’s the investors build and build and build until you’ve satiated the demand. And then, okay, lo and behold, we built a little bit too much. That’s what happened in Austin, Texas. Austin, Texas, built an enormous amount of housing, rents went down, and then developers stopped building new housing, because then they’re waiting for that amount of new supply to be absorbed by the marketplace. So I’m not of the view that if you allow private developers to build a lot of new housing, they’re going to build so much that New York City is going to become as inexpensive to rent an apartment as in Dubuque. That’s not going to happen. But you will mitigate this acute problem we have right now, number one. And number two, you’ll have a bigger tax base. You will actually have a more prosperous, thriving city, which is a good thing unto itself. And I think that there are some folks on the left who recognize that you need to build more, but I call this immaculate-conception progressivism. They say that, well, you can build more—provided you do it in exactly the right way, in exquisitely moral ways. By my exquisite moral standards. I’m not going to let you do it in some laissez-faire fashion, where the idea is that you build it to the point where you lose your shirt. I’m going to do it with you as a partner. Side by side, we will do this together, and I will essentially dictate to you exactly what it ought to look like. And I understand that there’s some subtleties here. There’s some complexities; there’s a question of getting from here to there. I get all of that. But I think that, fundamentally, if there are people who are willing, through their animal spirits, to address the problem, let them do it. Frum: How much new housing does New York need, in your opinion? How many units per year would put the city on the path to escaping from the crisis of affordability it’s in? Salam: I would say something like 50,000-plus new units a year, so that we would get something like half a million over the course of a decade. If you were to do that, then I believe housing would be much more abundant and more affordable than it is today. There are many other things that I would do too, David, but I think that that would go a long way. Frum: And how many is New York building now? Do you happen to remember? Salam: It’s more like in the kind of in the twenty thousands. You know, kind of maybe the high twenty thousands. But that is a little bit of an artifact of the fact that we just had a big rezoning, and also there are some units that are being built because of a tax credit that is about to expire. So people were rushing to kind of collect that tax credit. So those numbers I would expect to go down somewhat. But we’ll see. I think that our current mayor recognizes that this is an acute challenge, and he does want to build more. He, however, is not always mindful of the various other regulations that he’s imposing that make this a less attractive place to invest. So we’ll see. But we’re not anywhere near where we need to be. Frum: Now, urban politics, as you said, is inherently very complicated. People are close together; there are a lot of interests; there are lots of points of view. But one of the things that used to guide good decision-making was a few basic rules. And say, you know, I’m not going to master every complex detail. I just know if you build more housing, the prices go down. If you arrest more criminals, the streets are safer. If you sweep the streets, you’ll have less disease. And those basic notions, which are not a hundred percent true, but good enough—we seem to have a harder and harder time holding on to them. And maybe that’s because of something that I talk about a lot, and I know you think about a lot, which is the implosion of conservatism as a workable philosophy. It used to be the conservatives’ jobs to say: Build more housing; the price will go down. And as conservatives give up their ancient views and chase after new ideas—new and often quite sinister ideas—who’s speaking for these old truths? Build more housing; put the criminals in jail; sweep the streets; have schools locate kids with less economic opportunity and more talent and find a way forward for them. Who’s to speak for that? Salam: Well, first I’ll note that there have always been many conservatives who are small-C conservative, in the sense they want to protect their neighborhood, they want to protect its character. So some of that resistance to new building has always come from people who are small-C conservatives, who do not want the composition of their neighborhood to change and what have you. But the larger point is well taken. And you wrote an essay many years ago, David, that left a very deep impression on me. About how what you and I call conservatism reflected arguably an historical moment. When you think about the progressivism of the early 20th century, this was a moment; this was a sensibility that was a response to the challenge of urbanization, an enormous immigrant influx, and a pattern of industrialism that demanded new forms of state capacity. And then you had a progressive movement that was actually a part of both major political parties. In a similar vein, you’ve observed, there was what you could call a supply-side movement, a conservative movement, that actually did shape both major parties as well. And now that movement appears to be in abeyance. And what you have now instead is new forms of populist politics. You have a left-wing flavor of it; you have a right-wing flavor of it. And instead, the partisans of what you might call pluralism or classical liberalism or something that resembles the conservatism of that earlier era—they still exist. These ideas are still there; these ideas are still very compelling and relevant. But you could argue that they represent a minority faction in both of the major-party coalitions. And so what I would argue, David, is that I think that you need political innovation as well. You have a ton of new challenges right now that are markedly different from the challenges of even 15 years ago, when you and I were having that conversation about what had happened to the conservatism of that era of the ’70s, ’80s, and ’90s. And I think that those challenges demand new forms of left and right politics. And I think that’s a big part of what we focus on at Manhattan Institute. Frum: Well, let me ask you, since you’re kind enough to allude to my work. I’m basically at the end of my career, but you’re in the middle and peak of your career. You are going to have to ride your way through whatever’s happening next in American politics, which probably is a kind of collapse and discrediting of the ideas associated with President Trump. How do you find your personal way forward through this new landscape, in which it’s 2029, it’s 2030, the Trump era is left behind? Maybe the Republican Party is chased off under Vice President Vance toward evermore protectionism, evermore chauvinism, evermore xenophobia. How do you—and you have always stood for the opposite of those things—how do you find your way forward as a thinker and as an institution, in a landscape where so much will have changed? Salam: Well, David, I actually don’t believe that it is Donald Trump who is the only political figure who will have been discredited by this moment. When you’re looking at the Democratic coalition right now, I see a lot of anger and frustration with how people see their leadership class as well. So I think that this is going to be this big generational turnover that could go very badly. It could also go pretty well. When you’re thinking about the fact that we’ve had, I believe, it’s three American presidents who are all born in 1946, who presided over a period that many see as discredited. If you think about neo-socialism, this new movement, why is the term that had been so anathematized in American political life, why has it reemerged? One reason is because of that larger discrediting. And I think that in the case of Trump and Trumpism, what was fascinating about Donald Trump—and I’m talking about him in the past tense, but when he first emerged in 2015-2016—is that he served as a new coordinating device. There were many people on the right who felt as though they were burdened by backward compatibility. Ronald Reagan was still the figure that people could rally around. George W. Bush was a figure that many people felt they couldn’t rally around. And Donald Trump said some things, not entirely true, about how he had always opposed the Iraq War. It was a stupid war. And so he allowed himself to emerge as a new coordinating device. However, I think that that Trump era right now, in 2024, that campaign, I think, showed the outlines of what could be a new coalition. The problem is that the Trump presidency and how it’s unfolded did not represent the cementing of that coalition, that multiethnic coalition, a coalition that was—call it a back-to-basics coalition. If in 2025 you had a right-of-center presidency that said, We’re going to focus on inflation; we’re going to focus on getting the basics right; we are going to focus on having state capacity when it comes to managing immigrant inflows, managing law and order, this kind of thing. And we’re otherwise going to let the private economy roar —I think we’d be in a very different place right now. But President Trump, like many of his opponents, he’s someone who is very fixed on past rivalries. He is someone who is very fixed—you know, he has deep self-interest, he’s very self-motivated. That’s certainly true. And I think that basically you are going to have a very different politics in a few years’ time. It’s very unpredictable, what it’s going to look like. But I do think that some of these core ideas you were talking about, these kind of core pragmatic ideas you’re talking about, I think that they’re going to have a place in the other side. And I think that that’s something that everyone is going to have to be thinking about. It’s a reckoning that it’s not going to apply just to the right, but also to the left. Frum: Well, if we are turning the page, what writing will you put on that page? I mean, you’ve written two books about the way forward for conservatism at an interval of a decade. If you were to return to this at another 10-year interval, what would you say? What would you advise? Salam: Well, I’m fortunate in running a nonpartisan organization. We pride ourselves on our independence. We certainly have a point of view, but a lot of what I’m thinking about is identifying talent. Thinking about people who have a thoughtful, smart perspective on where things are heading and advancing a certain vision of American life. My view is that we have a multiethnic society. That’s just a reality that will be true one way or another, regardless of who’s in power. And how will we go about making that multiethnic society a success? And how will we ensure that that multiethnic society is in tune with core American values, and with core virtues that I see as good and valuable? When I came to identify with the political right, a lot of it was out of an appreciation for what Margaret Thatcher called the vigorous virtues: the virtues of independence, self-reliance, loyalty. These are just things that matter. They’re not the only virtues, but they’re virtues that matter, and they’re virtues that a system—a kind of government, a society, a culture—can either cultivate and celebrate or diminish and demean. And I just really believe that in our multiethnic society, there is a potential majority that embraces those ideals, that embraces the best aspects of our American, of our Western inheritance. And that’s what I’m really focused on. Just the idea of ensuring that these values survive into the future. So some of that is looking at policy issues through this lens. You know, trying to find what are novel issues that we ought to be paying more attention to that we haven’t.
